old: Elasticity is the property of a body to regain its original shape and size when the deforming force is removed. Plasticity is the tendency to retain the deformation. When a force acts, internal restoring forces develop. The restoring force per unit area is called stress, and the fractional change in dimension is called strain. Hooke's law states that, within the elastic limit, stress is directly proportional to strain. On the stress-strain curve, the initial straight portion obeys Hooke's law up to the proportional limit. Beyond the yield point the material deforms plastically. The maximum stress is the ultimate tensile strength, and beyond it the material reaches the fracture point. Ductile materials, such as metals, have a large plastic region. Brittle materials fracture soon after the elastic limit. Elastomers, such as rubber or the aorta, stretch a lot without obeying Hooke's law.

Hooke's law states that, for small deformations (up to the proportional limit), stress is directly proportional to strain. Brittle materials fracture soon after the elastic limit. Elastomers, such as rubber or the aorta, stretch a lot without obeying Hooke's law.
fixes: Hooke's law valid up to proportional limit, not elastic limit

old: A modulus of elasticity is the ratio of stress to strain within the elastic limit. Young's modulus applies to change in length, bulk modulus to change in volume, and modulus of rigidity (shear modulus) to change in shape. A larger modulus means the material is more elastic, that is, harder to deform. Steel is therefore more elastic than rubber. Solids possess all three moduli. Liquids and gases have only a bulk modulus. The reciprocal of the bulk modulus is the compressibility. Poisson's ratio is lateral strain divided by longitudinal strain. Energy is stored in a stretched wire, and the energy per unit volume equals half of stress times strain. For a wire under its own load, the extension is proportional to $L^2/r^2$. A given load produces more extension in a thinner, longer wire.
new: A modulus of elasticity is the ratio of stress to strain within the elastic limit. Young's modulus applies to change in length, bulk modulus to change in volume, and modulus of rigidity (shear modulus) to change in shape. A larger modulus means the material is more elastic, that is, harder to deform. Steel is therefore more elastic than rubber. Solids possess all three moduli. Liquids and gases have only a bulk modulus. The reciprocal of the bulk modulus is the compressibility. Poisson's ratio is lateral strain divided by longitudinal strain. Energy is stored in a stretched wire, and the energy per unit volume equals half of stress times strain. For a wire under its own weight, $\Delta L = \rho g L^2/(2Y)$, so $\Delta L \propto L^2$ and is independent of radius. Under an external load $F$, $\Delta L \propto L/r^2$. A given load produces more extension in a thinner, longer wire.
fixes: Extension under own weight is independent of radius
